Revised assessment incorporating economic-finance literature:
- Tone and stance: Balanced-to-slightly-hawkish. The Committee notes solid growth and a low unemployment rate but emphasizes “somewhat elevated” inflation and sustained uncertainty. Holding the policy rate at 4.25–4.50% while continuing balance-sheet runoff signals a restrictive stance consistent with rule-based guidance when inflation remains above target.
- Rule-based and flexible-inflation-targeting lens: In the Clarida, Galí, and Gertler (1999) New Keynesian policy-rule framework and the Taylor-rule tradition, inflation above 2% warrants a policy rate at or above neutral. The statement’s “balance of risks” language aligns with Svensson and Woodford (2003; 2004) flexible inflation targeting: risk-management around the dual mandate while data dependence remains paramount.
- Risk considerations from recent literature: Inflation-at-Risk work (e.g., “Mixing it up: Inflation at risk,” 2024) supports vigilance about upside inflation tails even as baseline uncertainty diminishes; this justifies the hold plus QT rather than an easing bias. Mention of swings in net exports is consistent with filtering transitory components in output gaps before policy adjustments in standard models.
- Operational implementation in line with post-2008 framework: Maintaining IORB at 4.4%, employing ON RRP/ON repo facilities, and continuing QT with caps reflects the modern operating system where interest on reserves and standing facilities anchor short rates (Federal Reserve, 2008–present). Continuing to allow MBS runoff and reinvesting excess principal into Treasuries is consistent with literature and practice that balance-sheet composition and size affect term premia and transmission to long-term yields (e.g., evidence on yield-curve slope sensitivity).
- Overall read: Communication acknowledges resilient activity but prioritizes disinflation credibility. Compared with a purely growth-focused read, academic guidance on rules and risk management tempers the positive tone.

Adjusted sentiment: mildly positive but more restrained than before due to the literature-backed emphasis on persistent inflation risks and the continued restrictive stance.
